subject: maths
title: Year 3 Fractions
seo_title: Year 3 Fractions Worksheets: Fractions of Shapes and Amounts, Number Lines, Equivalent and Comparing Fractions
standard_text: Recognise, find and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators; recognise and use fractions as numbers: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators; recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators; compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
meta_desc: Free Year 3 fractions worksheets for the National Curriculum: shaded fractions of shapes, fractions of a set of objects, fractions on a number line, equivalent fractions with diagrams, comparing and ordering, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The denominator is how many equal parts make the whole. The numerator is how many parts you have.
key_sub: 3/4 of 12: share 12 into 4 equal groups of 3, then take 3 groups, which is 9. For unit fractions, a bigger denominator means smaller parts, so 1/8 is less than 1/4.
body_html:
What a fraction means

A fraction is part of a whole. The whole must be split into equal parts.

PartWhat it tells youIn 34
Denominator (bottom number)How many equal parts make the whole4 equal parts
Numerator (top number)How many of those parts you have3 parts

A unit fraction has 1 on top, like 14. A non-unit fraction has more than 1 on top, like 34.

Fractions of a set of objects

To find 14 of a group, share it into 4 equal groups and count one group. For 34, count 3 groups.

Example

What is 25 of 20?

20 ÷ 5 = 4, so one fifth is 4. Two fifths: 4 × 2 = 8.

Answer: 8

Fractions on a number line

Fractions are numbers. They sit between 0 and 1 on a number line. Split 0 to 1 into equal spaces and count the spaces, not the marks.

When the numerator and denominator are the same, you have the whole: 44 = 1.

Equivalent fractions

Different fractions can show the same amount. They are equivalent.

Comparing and ordering

WhenRuleExample
Unit fractionsA bigger denominator means smaller parts.13 > 16
Same denominatorThe parts are the same size. More parts is greater.58 > 38
Example

Order 12, 18, 14, smallest first.

All are unit fractions. The biggest denominator is the smallest part.

Answer: 18, 14, 12

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking 18 is bigger than 14 because 8 is bigger than 4More parts means smaller parts, so 18 < 14
Saying 34 of 12 is 33 is only 14. Take 3 groups: 3 × 3 = 9
Counting the parts that are not shadedThe numerator counts the shaded parts
Calling unequal parts “quarters”Fractions need equal parts
Counting the marks on a number lineCount the spaces between the marks

faq.q: What fractions do Year 3 children learn?
faq.a: In Year 3 children work with small denominators such as halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths and eighths. They find fractions of shapes and groups of objects, put fractions on a number line, find simple equivalent fractions and compare fractions.

faq.q: How do you find a fraction of a set of objects?
faq.a: Share the objects into as many equal groups as the denominator, then count the groups in the numerator. For 3/4 of 12, make 4 groups of 3 and take 3 groups: 9.
Cut two same-size bars into 3 parts and into 6 parts. Each third is bigger, because the whole is shared into fewer parts.
A unit fraction has 1 as its numerator, such as 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8. It is one equal part of a whole.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is shaded?
items.e: The whole has 2 equal parts, so the denominator (bottom number) is 2. 1 part is shaded, so the numerator (top number) is 1. The answer is 12.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is not shaded?
items.e: There are 4 equal parts. 1 is shaded, so 4 − 1 = 3 parts are not shaded. The answer is 34.

items.q: What fraction of the shape is not shaded?

items.q: Which picture shows 13 shaded?
items.e: 13 needs 3 equal parts with 1 shaded. That is picture A. B has 3 parts, but they are not equal. C shows 14. D shows 23.

items.q: Which picture shows 34 shaded?
items.e: 34 needs 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. That is picture D. A shows 14. B has 7 parts, so it shows 37. C has 4 parts, but they are not equal.

items.q: Which picture shows 25 shaded?
items.e: 25 needs 5 equal parts with 2 shaded. That is picture A. B shows 35. C has 5 parts, but they are not equal. D has 7 parts, so it shows 27.

items.q: Does the shaded part show 14 of the bar?
c: No. The parts are not equal.
items.e: A fraction needs equal parts. These 4 parts are different sizes, so the shaded part is not 14.

items.q: Does the shaded part show 13 of the bar?
c: No. The parts are not equal.
items.e: A fraction needs equal parts. All 3 parts are the same size, so the shaded part is 13.

items.q: Does the shaded part show 15 of the bar?
c: No. The parts are not equal.
items.e: A fraction needs equal parts. These 5 parts are different sizes, so the shaded part is not 15.

items.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. George eats 3 slices. What fraction of the pizza does he eat?
items.e: The pizza has 8 equal slices, so the denominator is 8. George eats 3, so the answer is 38.

items.q: A bar of chocolate has 5 equal pieces. Freya eats 2 pieces. What fraction of the bar is left?
items.e: 5 − 2 = 3 pieces are left out of 5 equal pieces. The answer is 35.

items.q: There are 30 children in a Year 3 class. 13 of them have school dinners. How many children have school dinners?
items.e: Share 30 into 3 equal groups: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 children. One group is 13.

items.q: Kai has 20 sweets. 34 of them are red. How many red sweets are there?
items.e: First find 14: 20 ÷ 4 = 5. You need 3 groups, not 1: 5 × 3 = 15 sweets.

items.q: There are 24 pupils in a class. 38 of them go to football club. How many pupils go to football club?
items.e: First find 18: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. You need 3 groups, not 1: 3 × 3 = 9 pupils.

items.q: Charlie eats 14 of a pizza. Grace eats 16 of a pizza of the same size. Who eats more?
items.e: A pizza cut into 4 has bigger slices than a pizza cut into 6. 14 > 16, so Charlie eats more.

items.q: A cake is cut into 8 equal pieces. Mohammed eats 28 of it. Ethan eats 58 of it. Who eats less?
items.e: The pieces are the same size (eighths). 2 pieces is less than 5 pieces, so Mohammed eats less.

items.q: Oliver eats 12 of a sandwich. Isla eats 24 of a sandwich of the same size. Who eats more?
items.e: 12 = 24. Isla has more pieces, but they are smaller. They eat the same amount.

items.q: Amelia cuts a cake into 4 pieces. The pieces are different sizes. She says each piece is 14 of the cake. Is she right?
c: No, the pieces are not equal

items.e: Quarters must be 4 equal parts. The pieces are different sizes, so they are not quarters.

items.q: Aisha cuts a ribbon into 5 equal pieces. What fraction of the ribbon is each piece?
items.e: The whole ribbon is shared into 5 equal pieces. Each piece is 15. (4 cuts make 5 pieces.)
